articles.title: Stockholm Norvik port inaugurates aggregate loading facility
articles.summary: Ports of Stockholm has inaugurated a new port facility at Stockholm Norvik Port designed for the efficient loading of crushed rock aggregates onto bulk carriers, enabling large volumes of material generated during the port’s original construction to be shipped by sea to infrastructure projects across the Baltic Sea...
articles.body: Ports of Stockholm has inaugurated a new port facility at Stockholm Norvik Port designed for the efficient loading of crushed rock aggregates onto bulk carriers, enabling large volumes of material generated during the port’s original construction to be shipped by sea to infrastructure projects across the Baltic Sea region. The facility, built for NCC Industry and consisting of two pile-supported jetties capable of accommodating large bulk carriers, was officially inaugurated on October 16, though shipments had already begun in response to strong market demand. The removal of the stockpiled crushed rock will progressively free up significant areas within Stockholm Norvik Port, providing the foundation for new businesses and marking the starting point for NCC Industry’s planned business and logistics park. The initiative strengthens Stockholm Norvik’s position as a key logistics hub for Swedish imports and exports, complementing its role as Sweden’s newest modern RoRo and container port serving the country’s largest consumer market. Johan Wallén, Chief Commercial Officer at Ports of Stockholm, described the new facility as an important step in the port’s development, enabling more efficient aggregate shipments while unlocking valuable port space for new commercial activity. He highlighted the strategic location and extensive development areas as creating favourable conditions for businesses requiring efficient logistics solutions, with further development of the area to be pursued in partnership with NCC Industry. The facility also opens new opportunities to ship aggregates to additional markets beyond the Baltic Sea region.
takeaways: The facility also opens new opportunities to ship aggregates to additional markets beyond the Baltic Sea region.

articles.title: DACHSER extends Fraunhofer partnership to advance AI and robotics in logistics
articles.summary: DACHSER has extended its research partnership with two Fraunhofer institutes until the end of 2029. The collaboration will focus on artificial intelligence, robotics and digital solutions for logistics operations. The agreement covers the Fraunhofer Institute for Material Flow and Logistics (IML) in Dortmund and the...
articles.body: DACHSER has extended its research partnership with two Fraunhofer institutes until the end of 2029. The collaboration will focus on artificial intelligence, robotics and digital solutions for logistics operations. The agreement covers the Fraunhofer Institute for Material Flow and Logistics (IML) in Dortmund and the Fraunhofer Institute for Intelligent Analysis and Information Systems (IAIS) in St. Augustin, Germany. The partners will continue their work through the DACHSER Enterprise Lab, which brings researchers and logistics specialists together to develop technologies for everyday operations. “Our research collaboration with the Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft is a key element in our innovation strategy,” said Burkhard Eling, CEO of DACHSER. Digital twin technology reaches more logistics facilities DACHSER and Fraunhofer have worked together since 2017. One of their main developments is @ILO, a digital twin system that supports groupage cargo handling. The technology helps DACHSER manage cargo handling processes through digital information. It also supports greater visibility across logistics operations. DACHSER expects to have the system in place at 14 locations across Europe by the end of 2026. The @ILO project received the German Logistics Award in 2023. It also won the European Logistics Association Award in early 2026. Research to focus on AI and robotics The extended partnership will build on these developments. Over the next three years, the research teams will explore new ways to use artificial intelligence, robotics and digital tools in logistics. “The DACHSER Enterprise Lab, which marries scientific research with practical application, has proven its worth. Over the next three years, we will be focusing on digital solutions, artificial intelligence, and robotics,” said Stefan Hohm, Chief Development Officer at DACHSER. The research will focus on practical applications for DACHSER’s groupage network and wider supply chain operations. Through the partnership, DACHSER aims to turn new technologies into solutions that support its logistics network and improve daily operations.

articles.title: Port of San Diego welcomes ocean ecostructures
articles.summary: The Port of San Diego Board of Port Commissioners has approved a new Blue Economy Incubator pilot project with Ocean Ecostructures, a startup that has developed biodiversity regeneration technology designed to enhance marine life on human-made ocean structures. The agreement marks the 15th pilot project launched by...
articles.body: The Port of San Diego Board of Port Commissioners has approved a new Blue Economy Incubator pilot project with Ocean Ecostructures, a startup that has developed biodiversity regeneration technology designed to enhance marine life on human-made ocean structures. The agreement marks the 15th pilot project launched by the BEI since its establishment in 2016 as a launching pad for sustainable, ocean-based technology ventures. The two-year pilot project will be deployed across multiple locations throughout San Diego Bay and monitored for effectiveness, with the aim of enhancing biodiversity at port infrastructure without disrupting daily operations. The agreement is capped at US$ 208,000 in exchange for royalties on future gross revenues of up to US$ 1.25 million. Ocean Ecostructures has previously deployed its technology across Europe and the Middle East, and the San Diego collaboration marks an important milestone in the company’s expansion into the US market. CEO and Co-Founder Ignasi Ferrer described the partnership as an opportunity to demonstrate how marine infrastructure can actively contribute to restoring ocean biodiversity while generating measurable environmental and socioeconomic impact translatable into corporate value, providing a foundation for scaling the solution across US ports and beyond. Chair Ann Moore of the Port of San Diego Board of Port Commissioners highlighted the BEI programme as a demonstration of the port’s commitment to innovation, sustainability and its role as environmental champion of San Diego Bay.

articles.title: MPA Singapore and China Classification Society advance decarbonisation and digitalisation
articles.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore and the China Classification Society have renewed their Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen collaboration in maritime decarbonisation, digitalisation and talent development. The renewal took place during the Sixth North Bund International Shipping Forum in Shanghai,...
articles.body: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore and the China Classification Society have renewed their Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen collaboration in maritime decarbonisation, digitalisation and talent development. The renewal took place during the Sixth North Bund International Shipping Forum in Shanghai, building on the partnership established in 2023. Since 2023, MPA and CCS have collaborated with local research and industry partners on projects spanning the use of B100 biofuel on harbour craft and the evaluation, testing and verification of smart ships. Under the renewed agreement, the two organisations will expand research and development cooperation on decarbonisation encompassing green fuel value chains, marine electrification and energy efficiency technologies for vessels. Collaboration on digital and smart ship initiatives will also deepen, including digital testing and risk assessment for autonomous vessels to support maritime research and innovation. Both organisations will additionally collaborate on talent development through programmes including the MPA Global Internship Awards, the MaritimeONE Scholarship Programme and internships and attachments providing students and aspiring maritime professionals with exposure to international maritime companies and industry practices. Ang Wee Keong, Chief Executive of MPA, described the renewal as building on the partnership to advance a more sustainable and innovative maritime sector through expertise exchange and collaborative development of decarbonisation and digitalisation solutions alongside nurturing the future maritime workforce. Zhao Yan, Chairman and President of CCS, highlighted CCS’s ambition to make Singapore its most comprehensive overseas maritime technology centre and one-stop integrated service platform, framing the strengthened partnership as jointly advancing research and contributing to a robust, future-ready maritime ecosystem.

articles.title: US sanctions relief could lift tanker rates in Russia, inject capacity to Gulf shuttles: analysts
articles.summary: US sanctions relief on shadow-fleet tankers could redirect ships from Russian oil trades toward the Middle East, potentially raising Russian freight costs while easing some of the tanker shortages around the Strait of Hormuz, shipping analysts said. In recent public remarks, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US...
articles.body: US sanctions relief could lift tanker rates in Russia, inject capacity to Gulf shuttles: analysts in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 US sanctions relief on shadow-fleet tankers could redirect ships from Russian oil trades toward the Middle East, potentially raising Russian freight costs while easing some of the tanker shortages around the Strait of Hormuz, shipping analysts said. In recent public remarks, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US will allow legitimate businesses to acquire sanctioned tankers for non-sanctioned trades to reduce shipping costs, though Washington has yet to announce a detailed relief proposal. The number of oil and LPG tankers sanctioned by Western authorities amounted to 1,226 as of the end of August, with the US having been particularly targeting VLCCs, according to S&P Global Energy Horizons research. But BRS Shipbrokers estimated only 148 tankers in deepsea trades, equivalent to 2.5% of the global total by vessel count, were sanctioned solely by the US Office of Foreign Assets Control as of Oct. 19. Of those, only 14 appeared to have been idle for more than three months based on location signals. The “overwhelming majority” of ships that could become candidates for mainstream employment were therefore already deployed in likely sanctioned trades, mainly carrying Russian clean petroleum products, BRS said. That means sanctions relief could redistribute existing tanker capacity rather than simply release large amounts of idle tonnage. “It may not drive looser oil or tanker market fundamentals,” BRS said in a research note. “It would instead see more mainstream oil carried at the expense of Russian or Iranian oil.” Trade dynamics In recent weeks, shadow fleet operators(opens in a new tab) in Russian trades have often been making less than mainstream trades, where ship requirements have jumped on Hormuz disruptions. The average MR time-charter-equivalent earnings for the Baltic-East Coast South America was $15,518.14/day lower than the Global Clean Tanker Medium Range Index on Oct. 1-16, according to Platts assessments. Platts is part of S&P Global Energy. But Gibson Shipbrokers said tanker rates for Russian exports could increase if ships currently serving their trades were drawn into Middle East business. “The length of any waiver matters too, as a short-term reprieve may not be enough for charterers to commit to longer voyages, and the risk of renewed tensions after next month’s midterm elections [in the US] may further limit appetite,” the brokerage said in a note. Gibson said 84% of OFAC-only tankers were in the Middle East, Indian Ocean or East Asia, with just 16 ships in European waters. Their most likely employment could be Hormuz shuttle services, Gibson said, as recent attacks have constrained tanker supply. BRS similarly said previously sanctioned ships could prove attractive for cross-Hormuz shuttling, potentially easing pressure on mainstream tonnage currently performing such voyages. The VLCC rate for transporting 265,000 metric tons of crude from the Persian Gulf to West Coast India was $95.83/mt on Oct. 19, much higher than the pre-conflict level of $19.15/mt Feb. 27, according to Platts. BRS said some shadow fleet operators could also use sanctions relief to sell their tankers into the current strong secondhand market, provided Washington gave buyers sufficient assurances that they would not face sanctions risks over the vessels’ previous trading histories. The secondhand price for a 15-year-old VLCC has risen 177% over the past year to $160 million, while for a Suezmax of similar vintage it has grown 127% to $92 million, Xclusiv Shipbrokers estimates. Safety concerns remain A lifting of sanctions would not necessarily remove concerns surrounding vessels’ condition or operation, especially if they were still listed by the UK and the EU, where most third-party liabilities insurers and classification societies are based and whose authorities have not signaled any willingness to coordinate with the US on sanctions relief. Gibson said 70% of OFAC-listed tankers were at least 20 years old, including 120 of 163 VLCCs. Without International Group protection and indemnity insurance and classification by an International Association of Classification Societies member, few mainstream charterers would be able to employ them, it said. Removing an OFAC restriction is different from making a ship “genuinely acceptable for mainstream employment,” given potential obstacles including age, technical condition, vetting, insurance and charterer compliance requirements, according to S&P Global Energy Horizons analyst Fotios Katsoulas. “The pool that could realistically migrate back into mainstream trading is therefore likely to be materially smaller than the overall sanctioned fleet,” Katsoulas said. INTERTANKO, the world’s largest industry body representing independent tanker owners, also warned against treating legal sanctions relief as equivalent to a vessel meeting mainstream safety and compliance standards. “Lifting sanctions on cargoes, and on the carriage of them by these vessels, does not make these vessels any safer and adds risks to safety at sea, the marine environment and coastal states,” INTERTANKO said in a statement. The group said any return should involve scrutiny of vessel condition, insurance and ownership, arguing that lawful cargoes should be transported by properly maintained and adequately insured ships with transparent ownership. Separately, the International Chamber of Shipping told Platts that all shipowners should adhere to industry safety, environmental and insurance standards established by the International Maritime Organization. “At this stage it is difficult to assess the likely impact of the US proposal. A key element will be clarity on how this proposal will interact with vessel sanctions imposed by the EU and UK,” the ICS said in an emailed statement. Source: Platts 2026-10-22 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Ship Recycling Market Gaining Strength In India
articles.summary: The ship recycling market has gained strength in India over the past week. articles.body: Ship Recycling Market Gaining Strength In India in Hellenic Shipping News 22/10/2026 T he ship recycling market has gained strength in India over the past week. In its latest weekly report, Best Oasis ( www.best-oasis.com ), a leading cash buyer of ships said that “the Indian ship recycling market has strengthened over the past week, supported by an appreciation of the Indian rupee against the US dollar following measures and intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). The stronger rupee, coupled with improved activity in local steel sales, has provided a positive boost to the Indian ship recycling market. Overall, market sentiment in India remains positive, with currency movements and improved local steel sales supporting market conditions. The Bangladeshi ship recycling market continues to see strong buying interest, with buyers remaining keen to acquire suitable vessels. The availability of vessels in the market remains extremely limited, with very few suitable ships currently available for recycling. The ongoing shortage of available tonnage continues to keep buyers competitive, as market participants seek to secure vessels whenever opportunities arise. Source: Best Oasis Overall, the market remains extremely tight, with strong buying interest and a near-dry supply of vessels continuing to support competition among buyers”. The company’s report added that “the Pakistani ship recycling market has seen a decline in buying interest, with buyers no longer as keen as in previous weeks, partly due to some buyers having recently received vessels. The local market for ship plate and scrap has experienced a significant decline in offtake and prices, with scrap and wire rod prices falling by approximately USD 25–30 per ton in dollar terms. The main reason behind the recent weakness is the influx of goods from Iran, which is flooding the local market and putting downward pressure on prices. Recently, a damaged tanker reported to have been attacked in the Strait of Hormuz has also come into the ship recycling market, marking a notable development in the current market. Overall, buying interest has moderated, while weak local demand and increased supplies from Iran continue to weigh on prices and market sentiment. Finally, the Turkish ship recycling market has seen a decline of approximately USD 9 per ton in import prices over the past week. Despite the decline in import prices, the local market has remained stable so far, with no significant changes reported in local market conditions. Vessel prices have remained broadly unchanged, with no notable movement observed in the ship recycling market. Overall, the market remains largely steady in terms of vessel prices, although the recent decline in import prices reflects some downward pressure on the wider market”, Best Oasis concluded. Source: Intermodal shipbroker Meanwhile, in a separate report, shipbroker Intermodal commented that “last week, the ship recycling market showed mixed signals. India only reported strong sentiment, while Bangladesh, Pakistan and Turkey remained at last week’s indications. News of potential sanction relief for certain tankers may bring further candidates to the market, which could support recyclers and improve the outlook in the coming weeks. Alang firmed, lending a more positive note to sentiment. Local steel prices moved higher, although recent fluctuations suggest a price adjustment phase. Local currency gained against the dollar due to the recent interest and repo rate interventions of RBI in the economy. Waterfront activity is being sustained by vessels secured in previous weeks, as fewer candidates are circulating the market. In Bangladesh, appetite for available tonnage remained strong against a tight supply of vessels. Local steel plate prices rose. The pool of recycling candidates was also limited, yet a single bulker sale was reported to have concluded this week. On the macro front, IMF lowered its expectations of the country’s 2027 forecast GDP growth to 3.2%, aligned with World Bank’s (3.40%) expectations. Gadani remained in weak demand, with buyers still reluctant to make further purchases. Local steel prices held broadly steady, slightly below last week’s levels, while a surge of steel imports from Iran is adding pressure on recyclers. Rupee firmed slightly against the dollar. New candidates remain scarce, although a tanker damaged in the Strait of Hormuz has reportedly been circulated for recycling. On the economy side, following recent credit rating upgrades, Pakistan is in discussions with the US over a 10 billion USD facility to further support liquidity and foreign exchange needs. Aliaga remained stable. Local steel demand slowed slightly, with steel prices easing close to previous week’s levels. Lira weakened further against the dollar. No fresh sales were reported and candidates remained limited”, the shipbroker concluded. Nikos Roussanoglou, Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide Tops 2026-10-22 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: New and Established Yards Enter Tanker Market for the First Time
articles.summary: The list of yards building Tankers is widening, with a mix of brand new builders and established builders extending into the sector for the first time. Fifty-one vessels have been ordered for the first time at newbuild yards in 2026, up 34% from 38 in 2025, according to VesselsValue’s newbuild orderbook data....
articles.body: New and Established Yards Enter Tanker Market for the First Time in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 T he list of yards building Tankers is widening, with a mix of brand new builders and established builders extending into the sector for the first time. Fifty-one vessels have been ordered for the first time at newbuild yards in 2026, up 34% from 38 in 2025, according to VesselsValue’s newbuild orderbook data. Eighteen more-established yards have now received their first Tanker orders in recent years, with more emerging; Anhui Zhongrun Heavy Industry received its first Tanker order of a Handy recently. Yards breaking into the Tanker market Perhaps the clearest illustration of this pace is Hengli Shipbuilding, which built its first vessel only in 2024 and has since become the top Asian yard by orderbook size with 495 vessels on order — across Bulkers, Tankers, and Containers — and a value of USD 46 bil. Its rapid ascent from newcomer to market leader in under two years underscores how quickly new entrants have been able to capture significant order share amid the current capacity crunch. Geographically, the trend is heavily concentrated in China, home to 11 of the 16 yards, though single entrants have also emerged in South Korea, Vietnam, Brazil, the US, and Philippines. By sub-type, Aframaxes and Handy Tankers account for the majority of first-time activity. VLCC and Suezmax entrants, by contrast, tend to be established heavy-industry groups or joint-venture facilities, such as Wison New Energies Nantong (VLCC) and Guangzhou CSSC Shipbuilding Industry (Aframax, Handy Tanker, Suezmax), rather than genuinely new builders, pointing to a size-based divide in owner willingness to commit to unproven yards. Yards continue to take on Tanker orders outside their usual remit: Anhui Zhongrun Heavy Industry received its first order for a Tanker, 2+3 MR1 units of 41,000 DWT, set for 2029 delivery, from a Greek owner, with a VV Value of USD 38.6 mil. This follows a similar pattern seen earlier this month at Haifeng Shipbuilding, which received its first Tanker orders from Yangzijiang Maritime Development for two LR2s and four MR2s. There has been no notable pricing differential at Haifeng despite its lack of Tanker-building history. Why are owners choosing to build at new yards? Owners’ willingness to place orders at yards without an established Tanker track record likely reflects capacity constraints at established Tanker-building yards amid the current ordering wave. High orderbook levels support this, with 11.8% of the Tanker fleet on order, rising to 27.5% for VLCCs and 26.8% for Suezmaxes. In fact, Suezmaxes of 160,000 DWT have recorded the largest monthly increase, up 4.98% from USD 91.68 mil to USD 96.25 mil. Even with newbuild values elevated — and nearing all-time highs across all Tanker sub-sectors — owners appear confident that strong charter market conditions support a relatively short payback period on newbuild investment. What to watch as the builder base expands This combination of capacity pressure and payback confidence echoes, to some extent, the ordering enthusiasm of the 2000s, though the current wave is arguably underpinned by a broader base of owners and yards rather than concentrated speculative activity. Whether this expanding builder base can maintain delivery quality and scheduling disciplines at the pace current order volumes imply remains to be seen, but for now, the willingness of both owners and yards to look beyond established Tanker-building names shows no sign of slowing. Source: Veson Nautical Tops 2026-10-22 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Venezuela’s oil trade reopened. The risk moved to the vessel
articles.summary: Venezuela is not a binary, open-or-closed sanctions story. Trade responds to restrictions, but it also responds to waivers, licences and commercial incentives. For anyone shipping, financing or screening Venezuelan cargoes, the question is no longer only, “Is this vessel on a list?” It is, “What is this vessel doing,...
articles.body: Venezuela’s oil trade reopened. The risk moved to the vessel in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 V enezuela is not a binary, open-or-closed sanctions story. Trade responds to restrictions, but it also responds to waivers, licences and commercial incentives. For anyone shipping, financing or screening Venezuelan cargoes, the question is no longer only, “Is this vessel on a list?” It is, “What is this vessel doing, and what does the evidence say?” That shift is visible in the flows data. It is also visible at sea, where vessels can disappear from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), cargo can change hulls in ship-to-ship (STS) transfers, and activity can take place in ports and on routes that traditional sources do not show. Sanctions changed who could trade, not how much oil flowed Kpler flows data shows that Venezuelan crude exports averaged about 870 kbd in 2025, even as policy tightened. Sanctions policy changes who can trade and through which channels. It does not immediately switch off physical production. The break came in January 2026, when exports fell to about 667 kbd. That is a visible disruption, though not one that can be attributed to a single factor. Exports then rebounded. From April to September, they averaged about 1.14 mbd. The policy framework changed the commercial architecture around Venezuelan barrels. It changed which entities could lift, source, finance and transport the cargo. The flows data shows how quickly the market adapted. A timeline in which the same voyage can carry different risk Timing and licence scope matter, because the same vessel movement can carry different risk implications depending on both. • 26 February 2025: The US administration announced the wind-down of energy-related authorisations. • Following the announcement: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued general licences 41A and 41B, which moved joint venture activity into a wind-down through late May. • 24 March 2025: Executive Order 14245 created a discretionary 25% tariff mechanism for countries importing Venezuelan oil. At that point, it targeted China most closely. • July 2025: A restricted licence restored limited operations. Maximum pressure did not mean all authorised trade disappeared. Some permissions became more specific and more conditional. • 3 January 2026: The US operation Absolute Resolve removed Nicolás Maduro. OFAC then moved quickly to a controlled reopening and issued general licences 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 50A and 52. Licence 48 covered goods and services for the oil and gas sector, and licence 49 allowed certain investment negotiations. Licence 52 broadened the authorised transactions involving sanctioned entities within Venezuela. • August to September 2026: OFAC continued to amend these licences and ease some contract conditions. The framework moved from broad pressure to selective waivers, then to intervention, and then to a tightly conditioned reopening. Licence scope, vessel status and counterparty analysis now matter more. Where the barrels go, and who carries them The destination mix shows how routes change when the legal framework changes. In 2022, China and unknown destinations dominated. In 2026, the US is the largest identified destination, followed by India and Spain. That fits a licensing framework that brings more cargo into traceable commercial corridors. The risk has not disappeared. Unknown destinations, hubs such as the Bahamas and Curaçao, and STS flows still need review at vessel and cargo level. The vessel network is also changing. Kpler data shows more than 560 Venezuelan crude trades in 2026, involving 189 vessels. Screening therefore cannot stop at the cargo owner or the destination. A vessel can be absent from sanctions lists and still have high-risk behaviour or cargo history. Tanker capacity is also mobile. Vessels periodically associated with Latin American crude can be reallocated to other sanctioned or high-risk corridors, such as Iran. Risk should be assessed across networks, not single voyages. The AIS track is a signal, not ground truth AIS is extremely useful, but the quality of the underlying signal matters. Coverage gaps are more likely in places such as Venezuela. Messages can be delayed or duplicated. Positioning signals can be spoofed, and vessel identity and flag can change. Anything shown on a map should be validated before use. Three behaviours recur in sanctions-sensitive trades: • AIS gaps, or dark periods. A vessel goes silent around a loading area, an anchorage or another location. • AIS spoofing. A vessel transmits a route or position that does not match reality. Analysts test it against coverage, movement physics and satellite imagery. • STS transfers. Cargo moves quickly between hulls. The reason is sometimes operational, but in a sanctions context a transfer can also obscure origin or change the paper trail. These are indicators, not verdicts. An AIS gap can result from a deliberate switch-off, but also from coverage limits or technical issues. In the Strait of Hormuz, some vessels are switching off AIS to protect themselves against attacks. STS transfers are a normal part of maritime trade in many locations. What changes the assessment is the combination of signals. Analysts consider where the vessel was previously, what cargo it carried, whether satellite imagery shows an undeclared draught change, who owns it, whether it has sanctions exposure, and how nearby vessels behaved at the same time. A screening sequence that starts with the cargo A risk reconstruction follows a fixed order: 1. Identify the cargo and its origin. Is it Venezuelan crude, and where did it load? 2. Review vessel behaviour for AIS gaps, spoofing indicators and anomalous course patterns. 3. Check for STS transfers or dark events at sensitive anchorages. 4. Validate with satellite imagery and analyst review. 5. Only then assign an exposure risk indicator. A risk indicator is not a legal conclusion. It is a signal for enhanced due diligence. For Venezuelan-linked cargoes, four questions frame the screening: • Licence: Is the movement within the correct licence scope, dates, counterparties and destination? • Cargo: Is it direct Venezuelan crude, a blend or a re-export? • Vessel behaviour: Are there AIS gaps, spoofing indicators or dark events? • Network: What do ownership, management, flag, prior cargo history and counterparties show? List screening is where the process starts, not where it finishes. A vessel may not be designated and still carry significant risk. Sanctions are a political decision, so future designations cannot be predicted. The complete risk picture for a vessel and its counterparties can, however, be assessed against a company’s own risk appetite. What to watch next Four things matter for the months ahead: • Licences: New authorisations, wind-downs, reporting requirements and exclusions. • Destinations: Shifts in the balance between the US, India and Europe. • Fleet migration: Vessels moving between Venezuelan, Russian, Iranian and other high-risk corridors, depending on margin. • Behavioural spikes: Clusters of dark activity, spoofing and STS transfers around loading zones. Seeing more, earlier, with fewer false alarms The quality of any risk result depends on the quality of the data beneath it. Kpler owns and operates more than 13,500 terrestrial and satellite receivers worldwide, adds over 1,000 receivers a year, and operates 66 proprietary satellites. Its patented spectrum de-collision processing captures 10 times more signals than satellites without it. Intra-satellite communication brings latency down to seconds or less. The network processes over 1 billion AIS messages a day, at an average message frequency of about 20 seconds and latency of about 1 second. Because Kpler owns the infrastructure, it has direct access to raw data and can detect anomalies before the data reaches customers. In practice, that means seeing more, seeing it earlier and missing less. Denser data produces a more complete movement history, so gaps, inconsistencies and anomalies stand out more clearly. It also changes the analyst’s job. No team can search billions of positions for something unusual. Anomaly detection flags the exception, such as a movement pattern consistent with dark activity, an unusual port event, spoofing or a possible STS transfer. Analysts then confirm it and link it to a satellite image. Research teams face fewer false positives and spend less time on deep investigation. The same network, applied to supply chain risk Compliance is not the only risk that depends on seeing what vessels actually do. A shipping schedule shows what should happen, while AIS shows what has happened. Combining container tracking, vessel schedules and AIS gives actual arrivals and departures, port congestion and a predicted arrival time. The predicted time can differ from the scheduled arrival by three to seven days. In Latin America, ports are critical nodes. If congestion builds at Santos, Cartagena or Manzanillo, the impact can pass along the rest of the journey. Combining vessel arrivals, congestion, berth and port events and container flows shows where disruption is building, which cargo is exposed and when it is now likely to arrive. Average waiting time hides the worst cases. Switching a port view from average to maximum waiting time answers a different question: What is the worst delay to plan around? For four major Brazilian ports, the peaks can be significantly higher than normal operating levels and can move between ports over time. Aggregated data updates every 30 minutes, so changes in turnaround times can be monitored as they happen. The principle is the same for sanctions screening and container tracking. The better physical activity at sea is observed, the better the decisions that follow. Source: Kpler Tops 2026-10-22 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: The risk moved to the vessel in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 V enezuela is not a binary, open-or-closed sanctions story.
Trade responds to restrictions, but it also responds to waivers, licences and commercial incentives.
Sanctions changed who could trade, not how much oil flowed Kpler flows data shows that Venezuelan crude exports averaged about 870 kbd in 2025, even as policy tightened.

articles.body: FUJAIRAH DATA: Oil product stockpiles rebound as light distillates jump record 72% in Port News 22/10/2026 Oil product stockpiles at the UAE’s Fujairah rebounded 6.2% in the week ended Oct. 19, led by a record 72% jump in light distillates such as gasoline and naphtha, according to Fujairah Oil Industry Zone data published Oct. 21. Total inventory rose to 7.247 million barrels, marking the first gain in four weeks, the data showed. Stocks remain 65% below the Feb. 23 level before the onset of the Iran war, as disruptions to ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz continue. Fujairah is located on the UAE’s east coast, just outside the Strait of Hormuz. Light distillate stocks recovered to 1.304 million barrels from a record low of 760,000 barrels a week earlier, according to FOIZ data. The inventory increase was the largest recorded in FOIZ data shared with S&P Global Energy since 2017. Stocks of heavy distillates, used as ship fuel and for power generation, rose 12% to 3.682 million barrels, representing a two-week high, while middle distillate inventories declined 18% to 2.261 million barrels after hitting their highest level since the start of the war a week earlier. Since the war began, heavy distillate stocks have dropped 53%, while middle distillate inventories have fallen 23% and light distillate stocks have declined 87%. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed Fujairah-delivered marine fuel with 0.5% sulfur at $982/metric ton on Oct. 20, the highest since Oct. 13, while Fujairah-delivered high-sulfur fuel 380 CST was assessed at $739/mt, the lowest since Oct. 13. Designed to transport both LPG and ammonia, and with a dual-fuel engine retrofit option providing the flexibility to sail on clean ammonia in the future, they are built to serve today’s market while supporting the development of tomorrow’s energy transportation. As the new vessels join our fleet, we are strengthening our position in gas shipping and creating new commercial opportunities for our customers and Maersk Tankers. Thank you to everyone at HD Hyundai Samho and across Maersk Tankers who has contributed to bringing Jessie Mærsk to this milestone. articles.body: ENGINE: Europe & Africa Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 22/10/2026 Northwest Europe Prompt supply is tight in the ARA ports, a trader said, and buyers should allow lead times of 5-7 days to get competitive offers from a wide selection of suppliers, a trader told ENGINE. Verde Marine Energy said this week that it has added more barges to Flushing, Ghent and Ternuezen. The ARA’s independently held fuel oil stocks have averaged 7% higher in October so far, compared to September’s monthly average, according to Insights Global data. The region’s independent gasoil inventories – which include diesel and heating oil – have gained 6% in October so far, compared to September, according to the Insights Global data. Fuel availability is stable in Hamburg, with suppliers asking for five days of lead time, a trader told ENGINE. Bunker buyers are advised longer lead times of 10 days for supplies off Denmark’s Skaw and in Sweden’s Gothenburg, a trader said. Mediterranean Prompt bunker fuel availability is tight at the Gibraltar Strait ports, with buyers recommended lead times of 7-10 days to get good coverage from suppliers, a trader told ENGINE. Some suppliers in Gibraltar are delayed by 12-16 hours while some other suppliers are running 4-6 hours late, port agent MH Bland said. In Algeciras, some suppliers are running 24-32 hours late on deliveries, the port agent added. Suppliers need around a week of notice for deliveries in the Spanish port of Barcelona. Fuel availability is tight in Las Palmas, with buyers advised lead times of 7-8 days to get deliveries, a trader said. Rough seas, with swells higher than 1.5 metres, have caused a suspension in bunkering activities in the outer anchorage of Las Palmas, port agent MH Bland said. Operations can still be carried out in the inner anchorage or alongside berth. Due to lack of space, only one vessel can drop anchor in the inner anchorage at a time. Ships arriving first at the outer anchorage will be allowed to proceed first to the berth. Rough weather off Malta has suspended all bunkering operations there, MH Bland said. Deliveries are possible with a lead time of 4-5 days, a trader told ENGINE. In Istanbul, fuel availability is normal and deliveries are available with a notice of 1-4 days, a local supplier told ENGINE. Africa Bunker availability is tight in Togo’s Lome, and buyers are recommended lead times of 5-7 days for VLSFO and LSMGO supplies, a trader told ENGINE. FLEX Commodities said it has added a barge to supply VLSFO and LSMGO at the Lome Anchorage. VLSFO availability is tight in Nigeria’s Lagos Anchorage, and buyers are recommended lead times of between 10-12 days, a local supplier told ENGINE. In Luanda, VLSFO is out of stock with at least one supplier. The supplier said it can deliver LSMGO within 3-4 days. Fuel supplies off Namibia’s Walvis Bay are tight for prompt dates. Buyers are advised 5-7 days of lead time for VLSFO and LSMGO deliveries, a trader told ENGINE. Rough seas are expected for the next few weeks, with swells higher than 2 metres forecast intermittently between 21 October-5 November, which may disrupt offshore supply operations and limit all bunkering activities to within port limits. Fuel availability is tight in South African ports of Durban and Cape Town. Buyers are recommended 10-15 days of notice to secure deliveries, a trader told ENGINE. Fuel availability is very tight in Port Louis. Buyers are recommended to book 10-14 days in advance to secure supplies, a trader said. Bunker fuel availability is tight for prompt supplies in the Mozambican ports of Nacala and Maputo, with buyers recommended lead times of 5-7 days for most supplies, a trader told ENGINE. articles.title: EU lawmakers vote to create raw materials agency to cut reliance on China
articles.summary: The European Parliament has voted to strengthen the bloc’s Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), backing the creation of a dedicated EU agency and a €2 billion fund designed to reduce Europe’s dependence on foreign suppliers of minerals essential to the clean energy, defense and digital transitions. The amendments,...
articles.body: EU lawmakers vote to create raw materials agency to cut reliance on China in Freight News 22/10/2026 The European Parliament has voted to strengthen the bloc’s Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), backing the creation of a dedicated EU agency and a €2 billion fund designed to reduce Europe’s dependence on foreign suppliers of minerals essential to the clean energy, defense and digital transitions. The amendments, adopted by 470 votes to 83 with 108 abstentions, are designed to accelerate extraction, processing, recycling and substitution across the full critical raw materials value chain, with direct implications for commodity trade flows as the EU seeks to diversify away from dominant suppliers — particularly China — for inputs ranging from rare earth elements to lithium and cobalt. “Critical raw materials have become the currency of geopolitical power. Those who control them control our industrial future, our energy transition and our security,” lead MEP Mohammed Chahim, of the Socialists and Democrats group from the Netherlands, said. Supply security At the heart of the proposed amendments is the creation of a critical raw materials center as a self-standing EU agency, equipped with dedicated funding, clear governance and democratic accountability. The center will consolidate market intelligence, resilience planning, stockpiling coordination, joint purchasing, stakeholder engagement and financial instruments under one roof. MEPs have proposed funding the center through a € 2 billion Critical Raw Materials Fund, earmarked under the EU’s 2028-2034 long-term budget framework. The fund will provide revenue certainty to developers of extraction, processing and recycling projects through price-stabilization mechanisms, including contracts for difference, a tool already used in the European power sector to de-risk low-carbon investment. To keep recyclable materials within the EU and support domestic processing capacity, MEPs are calling for a conditional export-control clause that would allow the European Commission to restrict exports of permanent-magnet scrap and waste. Permanent magnets — which rely heavily on rare earth elements such as neodymium and dysprosium — are critical components in electric vehicle motors and wind turbines, sectors at the core of the EU’s energy transition strategy. The Commission, rather than individual member states, will be responsible for identifying large companies whose use of critical raw materials in strategic sectors — including batteries, hydrogen equipment, aircraft, drones, satellites and advanced chips — triggers resilience obligations. Those obligations would include supply chain mapping and measures to reduce vulnerability to disruption. MEPs also want the Commission to open applications for strategic projects at least twice a year, providing companies with clear and predictable timelines for investment decisions. Defense dimension The EU Parliament’s amendments explicitly link critical raw materials security to European defense capability, calling for the forthcoming European Defence Industry Program to be mobilized to finance strategic raw material projects vital to EU security. The move reflects growing concern among policymakers that supply concentration risks extend beyond economic disruption to national security vulnerabilities. The joint purchasing mechanism already available under the existing CRMA framework would be expanded under the proposed amendments to facilitate coordinated strategic stockpiling of critical raw materials by both member states and private-sector participants. The original CRMA was adopted by Parliament in December 2023, establishing an EU-wide framework to guarantee industry access to raw material inputs essential for the clean energy, digital, defense and aerospace transitions. The Commission proposed amendments to the law in December 2025, stemming from the RESourceEU Action Plan, citing the need to accelerate implementation and strengthen the EU’s strategic autonomy in the face of intensifying global competition for mineral resources. Parliament is now ready to begin negotiations with member states on the final text. Source: Platts 2026-10-22 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Panama Canal Authority The Panama Canal reported growth in vessel traffic, tonnage and revenue in fiscal year 2026, as stronger demand from energy carriers and containerships helped lift volumes despite ongoing concerns over water availability. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits during the fiscal year ended September 30, up 4.1% from 13,404 the previous year, according to results released Wednesday by the Panama Canal Authority. Total tonnage climbed 6.5% to 521 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons, compared with 489.2 million tons in fiscal 2025. Larger vessels continued to drive much of the growth. Ships using the canal’s Neopanamax locks accounted for 52.2% of total tonnage, with volumes through those locks increasing 8.2% year over year. The canal attributed the gains to stronger demand from energy shipping segments, solid containership performance and shifting international trade patterns. Financial results were even stronger, with total revenue reaching approximately $6.6 billion, up 16.6% from the previous year. The figures remain unaudited. The results come as the canal continues to balance growing shipping demand with water conservation measures designed to protect operations during the developing El Niño weather pattern. Despite the challenges, the canal maintained a maximum authorized draft of 50 feet throughout the fiscal year’s dry season, providing relatively stable operating conditions for shipping customers. “Far from restricting trade flows, the Panama Canal facilitates international maritime trade by providing its customers with a reliable and safe route,” Panama Canal Administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta said during a conference call hosted by Bank of America Merrill Lynch. The canal also announced Wednesday that it was immediately reinstating its Last-Minute Reservation service for vessels using the Panamax locks. The service allows vessels without existing reservations to secure a transit slot when one becomes available, although the canal retains discretion over whether to offer the additional capacity. The decision follows improvements in watershed conditions, with recent rainfall approaching average levels and water-saving measures helping conserve supplies. It marks another adjustment to operations following restrictions imposed earlier this year in response to below-normal rainfall. The canal recently increased daily booking capacity to 33 slots , including 10 Neopanamax slots, effective October 15. However, water availability remains a concern. The canal has warned that a continuing water deficit could require further operational adjustments, particularly if El Niño conditions intensify. During Wednesday’s call, canal executives also discussed longer-term infrastructure investments, including the proposed Río Indio Lake Project, a central component of the canal’s strategy to secure freshwater supplies for future operations. The project is part of the canal’s broader Vision 2025–2035 development plan, aimed at strengthening the waterway’s resilience and maintaining its competitiveness as global shipping patterns evolve. For now, the latest results show that the Panama Canal continues to attract growing volumes of shipping traffic, even as water management remains one of its biggest operational challenges. articles.title: The Navy Is Making Progress on Unmanned Vessels. Now It’s Time to Put Them to Work.
articles.summary: By Chris Servello (OpEd) After years of testing and debating how unmanned surface vessels fit into the fleet, the Navy is starting to show what these systems can do. And...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network An Arabian Fox MAST-13 unmanned surface vessel, attached to U.S. Naval Forces Central Command’s Task Force 59, conducts surveillance in the Arabian Gulf, Nov. 21, 2023. U.S. Army Photo By Chris Servello (OpEd) After years of testing and debating how unmanned surface vessels fit into the fleet, the Navy is starting to show what these systems can do. And there’s a lot to like. Recent operations in the Persian Gulf have demonstrated their value. The USS Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group has deployed with a medium unmanned surface vessel. Industry is delivering increasingly capable platforms. And senior leaders in the Department of War and Department of the Navy are talking less about the promise of unmanned warfare and more about making it part of everyday operations. That’s progress, and the Navy, its sailors and industry partners deserve credit. But now comes the harder part. The Navy needs to decide how it intends to fight with unmanned vessels, what missions they’ll perform and how it will organize, train and sustain the forces operating them. It’s time to move from proving these systems work to making them a routine part of fleet operations. Experimentation got us here. It remains important and should never stop. But experimentation alone isn’t a strategy, and continuing to treat it as one wastes time and money. The Right Signals From Leadership At this month’s Association of the United States Army conference, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth put autonomous warfare squarely on the department’s agenda. His Project Agincourt initiative and plans for an Autonomous Warfare Command are intended to accelerate how the military develops, buys and employs unmanned capabilities. Hegseth also emphasized something often overlooked in discussions about new technology: the need to change organizations, training and acquisition practices, not just buy equipment. The military has never lacked interesting technology. The challenge is turning it into something commanders can reliably use. Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao offered examples of where that transition is happening. At AUSA, Cao highlighted an unmanned surface vessel that helped recover two downed Army Apache aviators near the Strait of Hormuz. He also pointed to unmanned underwater systems supporting mine clearance and announced that the Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group had deployed with a medium unmanned surface vessel. These are meaningful developments. They show unmanned systems moving beyond demonstrations and into real missions. Cao described the technology as a force multiplier. That’s the right way to think about it. The goal isn’t simply more unmanned vessels in the water. It’s giving commanders more options, extending the fleet’s reach, reducing risk to sailors and freeing manned warships for missions that require them. The Persian Gulf Is Teaching Us Something Fifth Fleet deserves considerable credit for getting unmanned maritime operations to this point. For years, Task Force 59 worked with industry and regional partners to introduce unmanned systems into one of the world’s toughest maritime environments. Not every experiment succeeded, but the Navy learned how to operate these systems alongside manned forces, integrate their sensors and improve maritime awareness. That work is paying off. In June, when two Army aviators went down near Oman, a 24-foot Saronic Corsair unmanned surface vessel helped rescue them . The vessel recovered both soldiers and transported them to a location where they could be evacuated by helicopter. This wasn’t a demonstration. It was a real rescue, and two Americans came home because the Navy had the right capability in the right place. BlackSea Technologies, now part of AEVEX, offers another example. Its Global Autonomous Reconnaissance Craft, or GARC, extends surveillance and reconnaissance without requiring a manned warship for every mission. BlackSea also responded to an emerging operational requirement for unmanned mine countermeasure capabilities in the Persian Gulf. With mines threatening shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the Navy needed ways to address the danger without unnecessarily exposing sailors and expensive ships. BlackSea’s response illustrates the relationship the Navy needs with industry: identify an urgent problem, communicate the requirement and give companies an opportunity to deliver quickly. These examples matter for different reasons. Saronic showed what happens when an unmanned vessel is available for an unexpected emergency. BlackSea demonstrated how industry can respond to an emerging operational need. The Strait of Hormuz is an ideal place to learn. It’s crowded, geographically constrained and strategically important. Commercial shipping mixes with military operations, and threats can emerge quickly. It also reinforces a lesson worth remembering: unmanned vessels don’t have to be large, expensive or capable of doing everything. Sometimes a small platform performing one mission well is exactly what the fleet needs. But these lessons shouldn’t stay in the Persian Gulf. Fifth Fleet’s experience should help shape how the Navy employs unmanned vessels everywhere. Once a system demonstrates it can perform a useful mission, the next question should be how quickly we can get it to more commanders. Not how many more demonstrations we can schedule. The Theodore Roosevelt Deployment Matters The deployment of the Leidos-built Seahawk medium unmanned surface vessel with the Theodore Roosevelt strike group is another important step. Seahawk and its sister vessel, Sea Hunter, have spent years helping the Navy develop autonomous navigation, collision avoidance, communications and manned-unmanned operations. Now Seahawk is operating with a deployed carrier strike group. A carrier strike group isn’t a laboratory. It has missions, schedules and commanders who need equipment that works. An unmanned vessel must contribute without creating more problems than it solves. How does the commander employ it? Who controls it? What happens when communications are degraded? Who maintains it? How does it integrate with aircraft and surface combatants? What missions can it perform that free a destroyer, helicopter or aircraft for something else? Those questions matter. But they’re only the ones we know to ask today. One of the greatest benefits of this deployment may be discovering uses nobody anticipated. Put a new capability in the hands of experienced sailors and commanders, and they’ll find ways to employ it that engineers and requirements officers never considered. Maybe it’s an unexpected surveillance mission, a new way to extend the strike group’s reach or a task that would otherwise consume valuable flight hours or tie up a manned combatant. Some of the best ideas may emerge simply because Seahawk is available when an unexpected problem arises. The deployment will reveal problems, too. That’s fine. Better to find them during real operations than spend another five years trying to anticipate everything in a test environment. The Navy needs to capture both the expected and unexpected lessons and apply them quickly. Success shouldn’t simply mean Seahawk completes its deployment. It should mean the Navy comes away with a workable model for employing unmanned vessels across other formations, along with a better understanding of missions nobody originally envisioned. That’s how an experiment becomes a capability. And sometimes, how a new way of fighting begins. The Navy Needs a CONOPS It Can Man, Train and Equip To Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle has emphasized building a hybrid fleet that combines manned ships and unmanned systems. His fighting instructions identify scouting, screening and striking as important missions for medium unmanned surface vessels. That’s a good start. But the Navy needs to turn those broad missions into concepts of operations that commanders can execute and the service can organize around. Start with missions where the technology is reasonably mature: surveillance, scouting, screening, electronic warfare and selected logistics tasks. Continue developing more demanding missions, including strike and sea denial, as the technology and tactics improve. And resist the temptation to build one vessel that does everything. We’ve seen where that leads in traditional shipbuilding. Requirements grow, costs rise, schedules slip and the Navy waits years for a platform designed to solve every problem. Unmanned vessels offer a chance to do things differently. Establish common standards, define the missions and let industry compete to deliver solutions. Companies like Leidos, HII, Saronic and BlackSea bring different capabilities. That’s a strength, provided the Navy gives them clear requirements and a path to production. But the bigger challenge may be inside the Navy. Who owns these vessels? Who operates them? What training is required? How are crews certified? Who handles maintenance, spare parts and repairs? How does the Navy measure readiness? These questions aren’t as exciting as artificial intelligence or autonomous navigation, but they’re the difference between an operational capability and a science project. The Navy has started addressing some of this through dedicated unmanned organizations, personnel specialties and acquisition reforms. Now those efforts need to connect to actual force structure and deployment requirements. The service should be able to tell Congress how many vessels it needs, what missions they’ll perform, where they’ll be based, how they’ll deploy and what it costs to keep them operational. That’s what it means to man, train and equip a force. Keep Experimenting. Just Don’t Confuse It With a Strategy. None of this means slowing innovation. Technology is moving too quickly for the Navy to stop experimenting. Ukraine’s operations in the Black Sea have shown how relatively inexpensive unmanned systems can threaten much larger naval forces. The Middle East is producing its own lessons. Artificial intelligence, sensors, communications and autonomy will keep improving. The Navy must keep learning. But experimentation should improve an operational force, not substitute for one. We don’t stop deploying aircraft because better radars are being developed. We don’t keep destroyers in port while waiting for new missiles. We field what works, learn from operating it and make improvements. Unmanned vessels should be no different. Some systems will fail. Others won’t fit particular missions. Commanders will discover problems nobody anticipated. That’s part of developing capability. What’s harder to defend is spending another decade and billions of dollars experimenting without making the decisions needed to put these systems into routine service. At some point, experimentation without an operational plan becomes wasteful. And with the demands facing today’s Navy, wasted time may be more costly than wasted money. It’s Time to Make Some Decisions Secretary Hegseth, Acting Secretary Cao and Admiral Caudle have an opportunity to build on real momentum. The department is prioritizing autonomous warfare. The Navy is changing how it acquires unmanned systems. Fleet commanders are gaining experience, and industry is delivering capable platforms. Now the Navy needs a focused implementation plan. Within the next year, it should identify which missions are ready for routine operations, establish the organizations responsible for them and put the training, maintenance and sustainment systems in place to support deployment. Acquisition decisions should follow those operational requirements, not another round of disconnected demonstrations. Congress should support the effort while holding the Navy accountable for delivering usable capability. This doesn’t mean betting everything on today’s technology or choosing one company to build every vessel. It means making reasonable decisions with what we know and improving as we learn. The Navy has spent years working toward a hybrid fleet. Much of that work has been worthwhile, and recent developments suggest we’re closer than ever.

articles.title: Editorial: The Coast Guard Spent $3.8 Million on a PDF
articles.summary: The Coast Guard’s new credentialing portal promises complete applications and faster processing. One American ship captain tested it. What he found raises serious questions about automation, accountability, and whether Washington...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo of the USCG National Maritime Center The Coast Guard’s new credentialing portal promises complete applications and faster processing. One American ship captain tested it. What he found raises serious questions about automation, accountability, and whether Washington understands the problem it’s trying to solve. By an Anonymous U.S. Merchant Marine Captain Last April, President Trump signed Executive Order 14269, Restoring America’s Maritime Dominance . It’s a serious commitment to rebuilding the U.S. Merchant Marine, and tucked into Section 13 is an order every American mariner should care about: identify unnecessary or burdensome credentialing requirements and eliminate them. The White House understands something Washington has forgotten for decades. You can build all the ships you want, but without licensed mariners to sail them, they’re just expensive steel tied to a pier. Military Sealift Command has already had to scale back operations because it cannot find enough qualified crews. Anyone who has sailed aboard an MSC vessel understands what it means when a ship cannot get underway for lack of people. So when the Coast Guard launched NAVITA , its new merchant mariner credentialing portal, on September 14, there was good reason for optimism. As gCaptain reported in June , the Coast Guard tied the project directly to the executive order, and Rear Adm. Rob Compher said the goal was “to make it easier for mariners to get the credentials they need to work.” That’s exactly the right goal. For years, mariners have described the National Maritime Center in West Virginia as a bureaucratic black hole. This summer, more than 19,000 applications were reportedly sitting in the backlog, with processing times stretching eight to twelve months. I hold a Master Unlimited license. I spent over a decade at sea on tankers, containerships and MSC vessels, and I’ve been through the Coast Guard’s credentialing process myself. So I logged in and tested NAVITA. Here’s the short version. It doesn’t fix the problem. NAVITA does not appear to solve the problem it was designed to fix. The Coast Guard’s pitch is simple. NAVITA will speed things up by making sure every application is complete. It flags missing items as you go, it figures out your fees, and it connects to Pay.gov so you can pay on the spot. That sounds great on paper. The trouble is it’s solving a problem mariners don’t have, because the problem was never that we forget to include documents. It’s that the arcane and byzantine rules by which the Coast Guard governs credentials are so confusing to so many mariners that the information in the documents is often wrong. It’s paperwork that appears complete but contains information the Coast Guard will reject. And NAVITA, at least in its first release, appears unable to distinguish between the two. Talk to any mariner who’s been through a renewal and you’ll hear the same thing. Nobody forgets their physical. What trips people up is that the doctor has to initial and date every page, and a lot of doctors don’t know that, so the application comes back. Nobody forgets their drug test either. But plenty of mariners walk into a clinic and take whatever test the clinic offers, a 7, 9 or 12 panel, when the Coast Guard will only take the DOT 5-panel. Never mind that the other tests screen for more drugs, not less. Nobody forgets their sea service letters. What they don’t know to check is whether the tonnage on the letter matches what the National Vessel Documentation Center has on file, or whether the dates line up with the vessel’s records. Nobody tells you the evaluator is going to look. And nobody forgets to pay. NAVITA even has a fee widget to help with that. In my testing it gave me the wrong number, and more often than not it wanted me to pay more than I owed. So does NAVITA catch any of this? The answer is NO. It checks that a file is there. It doesn’t care what’s in it. That’s an important distinction when the entire purpose of the system is supposed to be reducing application errors. When I tested a renewal for a more complicated endorsement, NAVITA gave me a long list of “optional uploads.” Some had nothing to do with the application. Some were just wrong. Think about what that means for a mariner at home between hitches. The Coast Guard’s own website tells them they might need more training, so they sign up, pay for it and burn their time off doing it, for a requirement that doesn’t exist. Not really. NAVITA doesn’t check the data you type in. I entered an address that isn’t in the USPS database, and it took it without a word. That’s how your new credential ends up in somebody else’s mailbox. It doesn’t check your uploads either. It can’t tell if a scan is readable, if a page is missing or if you uploaded the wrong form. If the file ends in .pdf, it goes through. And if the tech team can’t get the if/then logic right on a fee calculator, how are they going to handle the much harder automation the Coast Guard keeps promising in the next release? I don’t have a clue. As gCaptain reported last September, the Coast Guard gave Stealth Solutions, a Salesforce consulting partner, a five-year deal worth up to $49.6 million to modernize credentialing . The first task order, $3.8 million, paid for the first release of NAVITA. Here’s what that first release does. It takes your information and turns it into a PDF. That’s it. There’s no back end. People familiar with the system tell me staff are re-entering the information from Salesforce into the NMC’s old system so evaluators can review it the same way they always have. So that’s $3.8 million for a PDF, with $45.8 million still left on the contract. The Coast Guard will tell you this is only the first release and the good stuff is coming. I’ve heard that one before. I shook my Magic 8 Ball on behalf of every mariner waiting in the queue, and it came up “Outlook not good.” And I have firends and family working for companies that use Saleforce. They tell me the company is famous for charging for additional unlocks. That might work for a large company raking in revenue but could cause an underfunded department like the NMC inside a budget anemic organization like the US Coast Guard to run into brick walls. From what I’ve been told, user testing was limited to a small group of service academy and union staff. A lot of them don’t work credentialing cases day to day, so they had no real way of knowing whether what NAVITA told them was right. Industry wasn’t brought in at all. The mariners and operators whose paychecks depend on this system didn’t see it until launch day. My two Navy friends looking to enter the industry after a career spent at sea on warships say they are thouroughly confused by the process. Uploads have to be PDFs. Not a photo, not a Word file. Just about every app on your phone can turn a picture into a PDF without you even noticing, but NAVITA can’t, because Salesforce doesn’t do that out of the box. Who owns a scanner in 2026? The Coast Guard will say paper is still an option. You can walk your application into a Regional Exam Center. There are 19 of them, 16 are open, and none of them are in the middle of the Pacific. And if you go looking for forms CG-719B and CG-719C on the NMC website, you’ll find the download links are gone. One friend who is caught in a doom loop was told he’ll need to submit a Freedom of Information Act request to get the contents of his file. So how exactly are mariners supposed to use the paper option? Credentialing is one of the most complicated things the Coast Guard does. Endorsements, sea time, medical standards and training rules all depend on one another. And the Coast Guard picked Salesforce, an expensive platform built to track sales leads, to run it. Anything Salesforce doesn’t do out of the box has to be custom built in Apex, Salesforce’s own programming language, which looks a lot like Java. Now the Coast Guard is locked in to one vendor, paying for every customization, and it still doesn’t have features you’d expect from any website in 2026, and they likely don’t have the budget to unlock the custom programing they need. There are also rumors circulating that Apex solutions is outsourcing work to Southeast Asia. Could the FBI background checks and the records of veterans be exposed to foriegn agents? Probably not but this is they type of question that could easily be addressed by USCG representatives visiting the gCaptain forum or providing regular updates via YouTube or social media to assuage concerns. A lot of companies handle credentials for their crews. They have to. If a mariner’s credential lapses, that person can’t work, and the ship may not sail. NAVITA only lets a mariner name an individual as a third party, even though the OMB-approved CG-719B form lets employers, unions and others do it. U.S.-flag operators crew the commercial fleet the Defense Department relies on for strategic sealift, so anything that hinders an employer from ensuring its crew is properly credentialed is a threat to strategic sealift. Employers can list jobs on the gCaptain job board but resumes have to be vetted and credentials checked before anyone is hired. NAVITA does not make that easy. And with so many US flagged ships doing critical national security jobs today, that’s a serious problem for our military. The executive order told the government to remove barriers for mariners. NAVITA adds new ones. Here’s my prediction. NAVITA will shorten the line in one way, and it’s not the way anyone intended. Experienced mariners who’ve renewed their papers for decades will take one look at this thing, give up and retire. A few years ago gCaptains founder Captain John Konrad wrote an editorial titled “ Admiral, I Am NOT Ready For War. ” His point then was that equipment doesn’t win wars, people do. That’s still true. We’re short of mariners right now, and every one we lose to a bad website is one fewer we’ll have when the country needs us. Editor’s note: This commentary is based on the firsthand testing and observations of a U.S. merchant marine captain who requested anonymity. Claims concerning internal Coast Guard workflows and prelaunch testing are attributed to information provided to the author and have not been independently established in this editorial. articles.body: Maersk has announced its latest bi-weekly Intermodal Fuel Fee update for inland transportation services across Benelux, the DACH region and Poland. The revised rates will apply from 26 October to 9 November 2026. Compared with the previous period, fees will decrease across Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Germany, Austria and Switzerland. Rates in Poland will remain unchanged. Region Countries Truck Barge & BCO RCO Benelux Belgium, Netherlands and Luxembourg 15% 15% 7.5% DACH Germany, Austria and Switzerland 14% 14% 7% Poland Poland 16% — 8% In Benelux, the fee for truck transport and Barge & BCO will decline from 16% to 15%, while the RCO rate will fall from 8% to 7.5%. Across the DACH region, the truck and Barge & BCO rates will decrease from 16% to 14%. The RCO fee will be reduced from 8% to 7%. Poland’s truck rate will remain at 16%, while the RCO rate will continue at 8%. The applicable percentages will be applied to Inland Haulage Import and Inland Haulage Export charges, known as IHI and IHE. The surcharge will appear as the Export Fuel Surcharge or Import Fuel Surcharge. Maersk said it reviews the temporary surcharge every two weeks in response to changing conditions in global energy markets. The company introduced the measure to address higher fuel and energy costs affecting landside and intermodal operations.

REUTERS/Nathan Howard The United States has imposed a new round of sanctions targeting a law firm, shipping agents and nine vessels accused of helping Iran move oil and other commodities through international markets, expanding Washington’s crackdown on the networks supporting Tehran’s shadow fleet. The U.S. Treasury Department announced the measures Wednesday as part of Operation Economic Outcast, an ongoing campaign aimed at cutting off Iran’s remaining sources of revenue amid the continuing conflict in the Middle East. At the center of the latest action is Karnakis and Karnakis, a law firm operating in Panama and Greece that Treasury says has spent years establishing shell companies used to conceal the ownership of vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, petrochemicals and steel. According to Treasury, the firm helped register shipping companies responsible for moving hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Iranian commodities, including vessels connected to previously sanctioned entities. The law firm also played a key role in establishing the corporate network behind Iranian liquefied petroleum gas magnate Seyed Asadoollah Emamjomeh, whose shipping operations have transported hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Iranian LPG and crude oil. Treasury sanctioned the firm and five associated individuals, accusing them of helping obscure the true ownership of companies involved in Iranian commodity shipments. The action represents a broader effort to target not just the vessels carrying sanctioned cargo, but also the legal, corporate and logistical services that allow shadow fleet operators to function. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that those supporting Iranian shipping operations would face consequences, saying, “if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you.” The latest designations also include Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading S.A., a Panama- and Greece-based company for which Karnakis and Karnakis serves as corporate agent. Treasury identified Roxette as the operator and ship manager of seven Panama-flagged cargo vessels: ANEMOS, GLORIS, PRIDE, DESTINY, FLAMINGO 1, HARMONY and PRINCE. Three of those vessels — ANEMOS, GLORIS and PRIDE — carried Iranian-origin goods, including petrochemicals and steel products, within the past year, according to Treasury. All seven vessels were identified as blocked property under the new sanctions. The department also targeted two shipping agencies accused of facilitating Iranian cargo movements through international ports. Singapore-based Amigoz Singapore PTE. Ltd. allegedly provided port services for an Iranian light crude shipment connected to Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company, which Treasury says helps channel billions of dollars’ worth of commodities to Iranian military entities. Amigoz was also linked to vessels associated with the shipping network of Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani and provided bunkering services to the previously sanctioned shadow fleet vessel ZIXUAN. Meanwhile, Dubai-based Whales Shipping Line LLC was sanctioned for its involvement with Amigoz. Treasury said Whales had also acted as a shipping agent for a sanctioned trading company involved in purchasing tens of millions of dollars’ worth of Iranian petrochemicals. Two UAE-flagged support vessels owned by Whales, WHALES DIAMOND and WHALES PEARL, were identified as blocked property. The measures are the latest under Operation Economic Outcast, launched on August 24 as part of the Trump administration’s campaign to isolate Iran economically. The effort has increasingly focused on the international network of ship managers, brokers, port agents, financial institutions and corporate service providers that support Iranian oil exports and sanctions evasion. Wednesday’s announcement also included a financial enforcement component. Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) said it was working with European partners, including authorities in Greece, to investigate a Greek bank’s potential connections to Iran and its proxies. The agency said it had issued its first administrative subpoena under a provision of the Bank Secrecy Act as part of that investigation, along with additional requests for information concerning banks’ relationships with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions. The latest sanctions come as Washington continues applying military and economic pressure on Iran, including efforts to restrict its maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
