Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Anita van den Broek Australia-based IFM Investors has agreed to acquire a controlling stake in Associated British Ports (ABP), the UK’s largest port operator, in a deal that values the company at approximately £10 billion ($13.4 billion). Under the agreement announced Wednesday , a fund managed by IFM Investors will purchase a combined 63.9% stake from two Canadian pension investors. Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) will sell its 33.9% holding, while OMERS will exit its 30% stake. The companies did not disclose financial terms, although Bloomberg reported that the transaction values ABP at approximately £10 billion, citing a person familiar with the deal. ABP operates 19 port facilities across the UK, including major gateways at Southampton, Immingham and Hull. The company handles approximately 25% of the country’s seaborne trade and plays a significant role in supporting Britain’s energy sector, including more than half of its offshore wind capacity. The acquisition represents a major change in ownership for one of Britain’s most important maritime infrastructure businesses. OMERS has held its stake since 2006, while CPP Investments joined the ownership group in 2015. Kyle Mangini, global head of infrastructure at IFM Investors, said the investment would support continued development of ABP’s port infrastructure and operations. The deal also reflects growing interest among pension funds and infrastructure investors in port assets, which offer long-term exposure to international trade, energy infrastructure and industrial activity. IFM Investors, which is owned by Australian pension funds and the UK’s Nest pension scheme, manages approximately £157 billion in assets globally. The firm already has investments in port infrastructure around the world. ABP has continued investing in its facilities in recent years, including the Immingham Renewable Fuels Terminal, Green Port Hull and Southampton’s Horizon cruise terminal. Henrik L. Pedersen, chief executive of ABP, welcomed the agreement, describing the investment as an endorsement of the company’s business and long-term strategy. He said ABP intends to pursue further growth opportunities alongside IFM Investors and its remaining shareholders. CPP Investments and OMERS said the sale would allow them to realize the value of their long-term investments and redeploy capital into new opportunities. The transaction remains subject to customary shareholder and regulatory approvals, including national security review, and is expected to close in the first half of 2027. articles.summary: By Julian Lee (Bloomberg) — Oil shipments from the Middle East are showing little sign of buckling in the face of Iran’s more frequent and damaging attacks on merchant ships in the...

Join the leading maritime news network The Soho Square, a crude oil tanker sailing under the flag of Liberia, is at anchor in the Galveston Bay as it makes it’s way to the Port of Houston shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a 60-day waiver of the Jones Act shipping law, in Texas City, Texas, U.S. March 18, 2026. REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian By Julian Lee (Bloomberg) — Oil shipments from the Middle East are showing little sign of buckling in the face of Iran’s more frequent and damaging attacks on merchant ships in the region. Crude and condensate flows from the Persian Gulf hit a high of 24.6 million barrels a day in the week to Oct. 18, according to data provider Kpler. However, shipments are volatile and figures for the average of October to date remain below prewar levels. Loadings tend to happen in bunches, with ships traveling in convoys through the Strait of Hormuz , shuttling cargoes to tankers waiting outside the waterway before returning to reload. Figures from rival data firm Vortexa don’t show the same weekly surge, highlighting the difficulty of establishing export levels as most tankers are currently operating with their positioning signals turned off. It pegs flows over the same seven-day period at 18 million barrels a day. Both companies estimate flows before the conflict was at least 18.5 million barrels a day. The continued strong volumes despite the Iranian attacks show the desire for Middle Eastern producers to keep moving their barrels. Oil forms the backbone of the countries’ economies and they’ve been competing for customers in recent months to make up for billions of dollars of missed sales during the conflict. For October so far, Kpler pegs Middle East flows at 16.7 million barrels a day, while Vortexa puts it at 15.4 million. Kpler aggregates its numbers from Hormuz transits, net flows via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, exports through Red Sea ports and those on the Gulf of Oman in the United Arab Emirates and Oman. The Vortexa numbers sum shipments from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Iran, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Oman. The resilience comes as producers including Iraq are sending more volumes through Hormuz while Saudi Arabia is sending oil out from both its Persian Gulf and Red Sea coast. The kingdom boosted production by a third in September to over 8 million barrels a day, recovering from the lowest in more than three decades in the previous month. The UAE, one of the most successful in moving tankers through Hormuz, has pushed its production to record-high levels, according to the International Energy Agency. These efforts appear to be holding up in spite of a spate of attacks in the waterway that’s also sunk at least one container ship this month. UK Maritime Trade Operations, a unit of the country’s navy, has reported 32 attacks on ships around the Arabian peninsula so far this month, compared with 16 in the whole of September. Some of these have struck ships’ engine rooms, inflicting more severe damage. “Attacks on merchant vessels around the Strait have increased sharply in recent weeks,” Morgan Stanley analysts including Martijn Rats wrote in a note. Still, “oil flow through the strait has remained relatively resilient,” they added. Shipments are proving strong with fleets owned by the producing countries and a few gutsy shipowners keeping crude flows close to last month’s levels that were the highest since the conflict began. The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait are among nations that have shuttled their oil through Hormuz in their own tankers, and delivered the cargo to customers’ vessels outside the strait. The levels are also significant because of the complete loss of Iran’s exports following a US blockade of the country’s ports. Both Kpler and Vortexa estimate the Islamic Republic was shipping close to 2 million barrels a day in February. The assessments of Mideast flows are subject to change as tankers operating in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea with their automatic information systems switched off make real-time tracking more complicated. The process is hampered further by the withholding of satellite imagery over the region. As a result, shipments are frequently only recorded several days after they occur, leading to upward revisions. The shuttling service and the tendency for tankers to move in convoys have also made exports lumpy at times, with brief surges followed by periods of relative slowdown. For example, satellite images of the biggest Saudi oil terminal in the Persian Gulf show five very large crude carriers loading at the seven moorings on Oct. 12 and 13, but the number had fallen to just one on Oct. 20. The pattern is similar at other oil ports in the Persian Gulf and on the Red Sea. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.body: The US Department of Transportation has awarded nearly US$250 million to the Alaska Railroad Corporation for the construction of a new freight rail connection to Port MacKenzie. The funding was awarded through the Federal Railroad Administration’s Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements Grant Programme. New rail connection to Port MacKenzie The project will construct approximately 32 miles of railway connecting Port MacKenzie with the Alaska Railroad’s main line. According to the US Department of Transportation, the new rail connection will support the movement of Alaska’s mineral and energy resources while improving access to the port from the state’s interior. The infrastructure is expected to reduce freight distances, shipping times and transportation costs. It will also aim to improve rail safety, network performance and service reliability. US Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said Alaska requires strong infrastructure to transport its natural resources safely and efficiently. The project is also expected to support mining, energy and industrial development while strengthening freight connections between production areas and Port MacKenzie. The latest investment follows a US$34 million allocation announced earlier in 2026 to expand the port’s capabilities. The Federal Railroad Administration also awarded Alaska US$28.8 million in August for the rehabilitation of the Hurricane Gulch bridge in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough. The project will extend the bridge’s operational life and allow train speeds to increase from 10 mph to 25 mph.

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Oil and Gas Photographer/Shutterstock LONDON, Oct 21 (Reuters) – Britain on Wednesday approved the Jackdaw North Sea gas field, ending years of legal and political wrangling as the Labour government seeks to balance its climate goals with energy security concerns. Energy minister Miatta Fahnbulleh said the project would begin supplying gas by the end of this month, helping ease energy costs that have surged during the Iran war. Higher energy prices have weighed on households and businesses, dragging on Britain’s economy and prompting US President Donald Trump to repeatedly urge Prime Minister Andy Burnham to expand North Sea drilling. The government said Jackdaw would raise domestic gas production by about 6% at peak output and operate for up to 11 years, calling it “a source of national strength” during a period of global instability. Jackdaw, at its planned peak production of 40,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, would cover just under 4% of Britain’s daily gas demand, according to Reuters calculations based on government data. “At a time when people are really struggling, it’s right that we look in a responsible way at maximizing the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help,” Burnham said. NEW ENERGY WEALTH FUND Burnham, who took office in July, has sought to balance pressure to tackle rising bills with demands from some Labour lawmakers to reduce fossil fuel use. Trump said on social media the decision was “Great news for the wealth and prosperity of the United Kingdom, and the wonderful region of Aberdeen.” Oil and gas production in the British North Sea goes back to the 1960s, generating tens of billions of pounds in tax revenue over several decades and was a pillar of Margaret Thatcher’s government. Hydrocarbon production has been in steep decline in the new millennium. Alongside approving Jackdaw, the government announced a new Energy Wealth Fund with an initial £2 billion ($2.7 billion) investment to channel oil and gas revenues into the transition to cleaner energy. The move aims to demonstrate that Britain remains committed to its climate targets despite backing a new gas project, following the country’s hottest summer on record. The Green Party called the approval “climate vandalism.” Fahnbulleh said bringing Jackdaw into production was compatible with Britain’s legally binding target of reaching net zero emissions by 2050. Asked about the bigger Rosebank oilfield, slated to produce 70,000 boed primarily of oil, Fahnbulleh said she had yet to make a decision. Both fields have been in limbo after climate activists successfully challenged their permits in the courts and forced the developers to resubmit applications that take into account the planet-warming emissions from burning, rather than just extracting, the hydrocarbons in them. “Jackdaw is a gas field that essentially caters for the UK market, so it’s gas that goes into our homes and businesses here. Rosebank is an oil field that is predominantly about exports,” she told Sky News. Even if both Jackdaw and Rosebank come onstream, their output would be small on a global scale and do little to slow the basin’s long-term decline. Jackdaw is run by Adura, a joint venture between Shell SHEL.L and Norway’s Equinor EQNR.OL. Shell welcomed the government’s decision. “Long-term energy projects depend on a competitive and stable investment environment, alongside timely and predictable regulatory decisions,” Shell said. REUTERS/Kim Soo-hyeon/File Photo The cost of shipping crude oil from the Middle East Gulf to Asia has surged to more than $37 per barrel, over five times prewar levels, as an increasingly complex shipping network keeps oil flowing despite escalating Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the International Energy Agency. The extraordinary increase comes as Persian Gulf oil exports have actually surpassed prewar levels, highlighting the steep price of maintaining energy flows through one of the world’s most dangerous shipping corridors. According to The Wall Street Journal , citing vessel-tracking data from Kpler, Middle East oil shipments averaged more than 24 million barrels per day in the week ending October 18, exceeding the prewar average of 23.3 million barrels per day. The recovery has been made possible by an improvised transportation system operating under U.S. military protection, including expanded pipeline exports, short-haul tanker shuttles through Hormuz and offshore ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. But the system is expensive, inefficient and dangerous. In a separate analysis published Wednesday , the IEA said tanker rates reached historic highs in September and continued climbing into October, with the cost of transporting crude from the Middle East Gulf to Asia exceeding $37 per barrel by mid-month. For a typical very large crude carrier (VLCC) carrying 2 million barrels, that translates to more than $74 million in freight costs for a single cargo, compared with less than $15 million before the conflict. The surge reflects a fundamental shift in how oil moves out of the Gulf. Before the war, approximately 17% of the region’s crude exports bypassed Hormuz. By September, that share had climbed to 40%, according to Kpler, as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates expanded the use of pipelines to export terminals outside the strait. Meanwhile, tankers continue making dangerous runs through Hormuz, often traveling along a corridor near the Omani coast under American military protection before transferring their cargoes to other vessels for delivery to international markets. Despite the recovery in overall exports, oil flows through Hormuz, including offshore transfers, remain at approximately 82% of prewar levels. The shipping system has become increasingly resilient even as attacks intensify. The Wall Street Journal reported approximately 30 attacks on vessels so far in October, citing maritime security reports. Those risks have brought extraordinary financial incentives. Kpler estimates that traders can earn an additional $20 per barrel reselling Iraqi crude compared with before the war, while some seafarers are being offered substantial hazard bonuses to make the crossings. The result is a market in which oil is moving in greater volumes, but at a significantly higher cost to the companies transporting, refining and ultimately consuming it. articles.body: Regional Container Lines (RCL) will introduce an Advance Filing Surcharge as part of its compliance with the United Arab Emirates’ Maritime Preload Cargo Information (MPCI) programme. The regulatory framework, also known as the Advance Manifest Filing requirement, requires shipping lines to submit import cargo manifest data electronically to UAE Customs before vessels depart from their last foreign port outside the country. Shipments covered by the MPCI programme The mandatory filing requirement applies to all containerised maritime cargo entering or passing through UAE ports, including: Local imports destined for clearance in the UAE Transshipment cargo discharged in the UAE for onward connection Transit and Freight Remaining on Board cargo passing through the UAE without discharge Shipping Instruction deadline Customers must submit complete and accurate Shipping Instructions or Bill of Lading drafts no later than 48 hours before the vessel’s estimated arrival at the port of loading. RCL warned that incomplete or late submissions could result in cargo being rolled or receiving a Do Not Load instruction from UAE Customs. Advance filing surcharge The new charge will apply from 16 October 2026, based on the vessel’s departure date at origin. Charge code Charge Scope Currency Amount Basis 42910 Advance Filing Surcharge Import, transshipment, transit and FROB USD 17 Per Bill of Lading RCL said the surcharge will cover the preparation, processing and electronic transmission of the required shipment information.

REUTERS/Stringer Two more tankers have been struck by unidentified projectiles in separate incidents near the Strait of Hormuz and in the northern Persian Gulf, adding to a growing series of attacks on commercial shipping as maritime security conditions across the region continue to deteriorate. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported Wednesday that a tanker was struck approximately 11 nautical miles west of Bukha, Oman, at 0145 UTC on October 21. The impact sparked a fire aboard the vessel, which has since been extinguished. The tanker is now at anchor, with all crew members reported safe and no environmental damage reported. In a separate incident, the master of another tanker reported being struck by an unknown projectile approximately 30 nautical miles southeast of Al Faw, Iraq, at 1830 UTC on October 20. UKMTO received the report after the incident occurred. All crew members were reported safe, with no damage to the vessel or environmental impact reported. Neither vessel has been publicly identified, and UKMTO did not attribute responsibility for either attack. The latest incidents come amid a sharp increase in attacks against commercial shipping, with violence increasingly extending beyond the Strait of Hormuz into the wider Persian Gulf. In its October 18 advisory , the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) maintained its SEVERE threat assessment for the Strait of Hormuz, warning that deliberate attacks remained highly likely. The assessment followed a particularly violent period in which UKMTO recorded 12 attacks on commercial vessels during the week ending October 16, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz, one in the Persian Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. JMIC reported 153 confirmed maritime security incidents across the region since March 1, a figure that predates the latest attacks. Recent incidents have also demonstrated the growing danger to vessels operating away from the strait’s main shipping lanes. On October 16, two tankers were attacked near Al Jubayl, Saudi Arabia, including one struck by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat. Another tanker was hit by an unidentified projectile, forcing its crew to evacuate. On October 18, a tug operating approximately 20 nautical miles northeast of Khor Fakkan, UAE, was struck by two projectiles. The vessel sustained damage but was able to continue its voyage, with one minor crew injury reported. JMIC subsequently raised the threat level for the wider Persian Gulf to SUBSTANTIAL , citing the expanding pattern of attacks and growing electronic navigation interference. The advisory also warned that vessels remaining stationary for extended periods, particularly those broadcasting AIS signals, could face increased targeting risks. The threat is becoming particularly concerning around major anchorages. As of October 18, JMIC counted approximately 217 vessels anchored near Fujairah and Khor Fakkan, with another 166 in waters stretching from Dubai and Jebel Ali toward Ras Al Khaimah. The latest attacks also follow renewed Iranian claims that commercial vessels have struck sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz. On October 17, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy claimed that two supertankers had struck mines in the waterway. JMIC said there was no substantiation for those claims. Although JMIC continues to warn mariners about possible mining activity in and around the strait’s traffic separation scheme, the two latest UKMTO warnings describe strikes by unidentified projectiles, not confirmed mine explosions. articles.summary: Poland has hit a new milestone in its energy independence journey, completing the foundational piling for the new FSRU terminal in Gdańsk.
articles.body: Business Developments & Projects October 21, 2026 · 12 hours ago Over 500 piles lay the foundation for Poland’s floating LNG terminal (Gallery) Poland has hit a new milestone in its energy independence journey, completing the foundational piling for the new FSRU terminal in Gdańsk. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 4 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Completion of the installation of over 500 piles forming the foundation of the quay for the floating LNG terminal in Gdańsk Bay Source: Gaz-System With more than 500 massive steel piles now hammered into place on time and on budget, Poland’s gas transmission system operator (TSO), Gaz-System, has cleared a critical hurdle for the country's upcoming floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) in Gdańsk. This work lays the physical bedrock for a project designed to rewrite Poland's energy playbook, bringing the nation one step closer to welcoming its first FSRU vessel by early 2028. GAZ-SYSTEM has completed the driving of more than 500 piles forming the foundation of the jetty for the FSRU terminal in the Gulf of Gdańsk in accordance with the approved schedule, said to be completed on time and on budget as a key phase in the project to enable Poland to make inroads in launching the second liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal on the Polish coast. Miłosz Motyka , Minister for Energy, commented: “Developing LNG infrastructure directly strengthens Poland by securing its energy supply, boosting the economy, and upgrading the country’s position across Europe. The FSRU terminal in Gdańsk will increase our capacity to import natural gas from global markets and bolster Poland’s role in the regional supply system. “This project is of particular importance considering ongoing geopolitical tensions and the evolving dynamics of the energy landscape. The significance of strategic investment projects extends beyond the energy sector itself – they also provide a boost to Polish businesses, harness domestic expertise and lay the foundations for stable development conditions for industry and the economy as a whole.” Related Articles Clean Fuel With environmental decision in place, GAZ-SYSTEM set to proceed with Gdańsk FSRU project 3 min read The installed piles form the basis of the jetty structure and will support the platforms and enable the installation of all the equipment and systems necessary to operate the FSRUs. The construction of the offshore section of the project involves the consortium of companies, including FABE Polska . Wojciech Wrochna , Secretary of State at the Ministry of Energy and the Government Plenipotentiary for Strategic Energy Infrastructure, said: “ The completion of pile driving operation for the jetty in the FSRU Terminal in Gdańsk marks another step towards the commissioning of a new gas supply facility in Poland. “This initiative will effectively increase our gas import capacity by sea, reinforce supply diversification, and create additional opportunities for adaptable response to domestic energy demand. We remain committed to delivering investment projects that enhance the resilience and competitiveness of the Polish economy, thereby reinforcing our energy independence .” In parallel with the jetty construction, Gaz-System underlines that operations continue to integrate the offshore and onshore parts of the facility, with August 2026 marking the drilling of a microtunnel over a kilometer in length, routed under the forest, dunes, and beach in Górki Zachodnie. We faced difficult conditions and changeable weather conditions. “Nevertheless, owing to the determination of the contractors and meticulous coordination of the works, we have reached this critical milestone within the planned timeline. Now, the terminal features a robust physical foundation. Next, we will be assembling the platforms and preparing for the construction of the subsea gas pipeline .” A specialized tunnel boring machine (TBM) remained beneath the Baltic Sea seabed following the drilling operation, as it was used for the construction; thus, preparations are now in progress to facilitate its retrieval. A gas pipeline will be laid inside the tunnel connecting the terminal to the onshore part of the facility. The work on the onshore section is also well advanced, as the Gdańsk–Gustorzyn gas pipeline underwent tests in September, which is reported to have confirmed a high standard of work and the pipeline’s good working order. Łukasz Radomski , Deputy Contract Director at GAP–FABE–UNITEK Consortium, underscored: “ The steel piles driven into the seabed of the Gulf of Gdańsk form the foundation of the structure on which the prefabricated jetty platforms will be mounted along with necessary equipment. Concurrently, a microtunnel spanning over one kilometer was completed, designed for the installation of the gas pipeline connecting the offshore facility to the onshore system. “The greatest challenge was the seamless coordination of all operation components in one place and at one time; the delivery of materials, the availability of vessels and specialist equipment, and the work of teams at sea and on land. It was precisely this highly efficient logistical framework that enabled us to incorporate engineering solutions into timely project delivery.” Meanwhile, works are underway to complete the outfitting of the FSRU at the South Korean shipyard in Ulsan, with commissioning scheduled for early 2028. Following the regasification process, natural gas from the Solidarity vessel will be delivered to customers. articles.summary: Woodside’s Scarborough, Trion, and Louisiana LNG projects have hit new milestones, with the finish line in sight for the first one.
articles.body: Business Developments & Projects October 21, 2026 · 14 hours ago Australian gas project enters home stretch as developments in Mexico and US Gulf make new inroads Woodside’s Scarborough, Trion, and Louisiana LNG projects have hit new milestones, with the finish line in sight for the first one. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Delivery of Pluto LNG module for Scarborough gas project Source: Woodside While navigating complex supply chains to deliver its projects in line with established timelines, Australia’s energy giant Woodside has advanced three major projects spanning the waters offshore Western Australia, where the almost complete Scarborough mega-project is rushing toward its first liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipment, along with deepwater milestones in Mexico and resilient construction in the U.S. Gulf. Woodside has provided updates on the progress made in developing three projects, including Scarborough offshore Australia, Trion in Mexican waters, and Louisiana LNG in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America). The Scarborough and Pluto Train 2 projects remain on budget and were 99% complete at the end of the third quarter of 2026, excluding Pluto Train 1 modifications. The floating production unit (FPU) and subsea production system commissioning and start-up activities continued, including well clean-up and export of gas to pressurise the trunkline. The operator emphasizes that well clean-up results are in line with reservoir and well performance expectations. articles.body: Uncategorized AG Seville wins 25-year port shipyard concession with $11m investment plan Splash Ports October 21, 2026 0 92 1 minute read AG Seville Shipyard AG Seville Shipyard AG Seville Shipyard has won the competition to continue operating the ship repair facilities at Spain’s Port of Seville, clearing an important hurdle for a proposed €10m ($11.2m) investment programme. Seville Port Authority’s board approved the selection of AG Seville Shipyard on October 20, allowing the company to retain its position at the former Astilleros del Guadalquivir facilities. The operator’s existing concession expires in December.The new concession will cover approximately 22,000 sq m of port land and infrastructure, including the dry dock, the southern section of the Muelle de Armamento and a disused slipway. The concession can run for up to 25 years, although final administrative approval is still required before the new agreement becomes effective. AG Seville Shipyard faced competition for the facilities from Spanish maritime group Boluda, which had also expressed interest in taking over the site. The successful operator has controlled part of the former Seville shipyard since 2017, developing ship repair and maintenance operations at facilities that had suffered years of decline following the collapse of the former public shipyard. The company plans to invest approximately €10m ($11.2m) in modernisation and expansion projects under the new concession. The tender conditions also require the successful operator to invest at least €3m ($3.4m) during the first three years, including improvements to the slipway and dry dock infrastructure. The larger €10m programme is AG Seville’s proposed investment plan, rather than an amount separately confirmed as contractually committed in the latest announcement. The port authority also approved an additional €4.2m ($4.7m) for improvements to Seville’s port free zone. The decision raises the total budget for modernising the area to €8m ($9m), covering electrical infrastructure, roads, lighting and other facilities serving businesses operating within the port’s industrial zone. The port authority will oversee procurement and technical management of the improvement projects. OMERS was part of the consortium that took ABP private in 2006 for £2.8bn, while CPP Investments acquired its interest in 2015. Singapore sovereign wealth fund GIC and Kuwait’s Wren House Infrastructure remain among the group’s minority investors. IFM is owned by Australian and British pension funds and manages around $96bn in infrastructure assets globally. The acquisition comes as ABP pursues substantial investment across its network. articles.title: Norway set on tapping into Arctic gas potential: New study to unlock 1988 Barents Sea discovery
articles.summary: Norway is targeting untapped Arctic energy by commissioning a new study to shed more light on the 1988 gas discovery in the Barents Sea.
articles.body: Exploration & Production October 21, 2026 · 18 hours ago Norway set on tapping into Arctic gas potential: New study to unlock 1988 Barents Sea discovery Norway is targeting untapped Arctic energy by commissioning a new study to shed more light on the 1988 gas discovery in the Barents Sea. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Credit: Morten Berentsen/Norwegian Offshore Directorate Decades after being left behind in the frozen depths of the High North, a forgotten 1980s gas find in the Barents Sea is getting a second look. As Europe hungers for new energy sources and low-carbon reserves, Norway is launching a fresh push to unlock the untapped potential of the Arctic, starting with a neglected discovery 200 kilometers north of the Arctic Circle. The Barents Sea is home to a number of discoveries that could hold vast volumes of gas but remains less explored than other parts of the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS), with several discoveries in these waters potentially containing significant volumes of gas, according to the Norwegian Offshore Directorate, which emphasizes that a new study could uncover major opportunities for one of these discoveries. The gas discovery that this study will aim to gain more insight into is Norselhøgda (the well 7226/11-1 ), which is situated about 200 kilometers north of Hammerfest and was made in 1988. The discovery was production-tested, but the acreage was subsequently relinquished to the authorities. Arne Jacobsen , Assistant Director for Technology and Subsurface, commented: “Several major gas discoveries have been made in the Barents Sea which we still don’t know much about. Norselhøgda is one of a number of discoveries the Norwegian Offshore Directorate believes the companies should take a closer look at.” The Norwegian Offshore Directorate has hired the consulting company Terra Stream Energy to carry out a study that could bring new knowledge about the more precise volume of recoverable resources in the discovery. The reservoir is tight and will probably require stimulation . This is technology that is already being used on the NCS and elsewhere in the world. “The objective is to develop a model that can be shared with the companies so they can make further assessments of mapping and technologies that could help realize a potential development,” added Jacobsen. The study is scheduled to be completed towards the end of this year. In connection with this, the Norwegian Offshore Directorate plans to share the model and hold a professional seminar for the industry. Several comparable discoveries have been made in the area, which include production license 1313 , located to the north of the Norselhøgda discovery and awarded in APA 2025 . The Gro discovery in the Norwegian Sea is another discovery the Norwegian Offshore Directorate hopes to revive, along with the Linerle discovery in the Norwegian Sea. Related Articles Fossil Energy $1.42 trillion at stake as oil & gas production ebbs away: Norway urged to pick up the pace of exploration and tech advancement 3 min read “It’s possible that these discoveries could be viewed in an overall context. There could be benefits to extract if 1313 is developed further. The companies will have an opportunity to apply for Norselhøgda in the next APA round,” noted Jacobsen. The resource potential in the Barents Sea is considered to be considerable, as extensive parts of it remain largely unexplored, with significant acreage that has yet to be opened up for petroleum activity; thus, the development of this potential rests on the development of infrastructure and is particularly relevant for increased gas export opportunities. “Realizing Norselhøgda could be one step towards bringing this all into place,” underlined Jacobsen, while pointing out that the gas proven in the area has a very low CO2 content, just 0.3%, and development and production of gas with such low CO2 content provides added flexibility in exploiting existing infrastructure. articles.title: Shipping equities turn geopolitical risk into an advantage
articles.summary: New research from investment bank Jefferies charts how shipping shares have shifted from being negatively correlated with geopolitical risk during the first decade of this century to moving increasingly in tandem with global instability since 2021. The new report is bullish on tankers, predicting that shares have...
articles.body: Containers Dry Cargo Gas Tankers Shipping equities turn geopolitical risk into an advantage Sam Chambers October 21, 2026 0 826 2 minutes read Photo by Aditya Vyas on Unsplash Photo by Aditya Vyas on Unsplash New research from investment bank Jefferies charts how shipping shares have shifted from being negatively correlated with geopolitical risk during the first decade of this century to moving increasingly in tandem with global instability since 2021. The new report is bullish on tankers, predicting that shares have further room to run, with rates forecast to taper more slowly than the market currently anticipates, in no small part down to the geopolitical correlation. “Since 2021, shipping stocks have also moved with our Geopolitical Risk Index every year, and we expect owners to keep capitalizing on the dislocation into 2027/2028+,” the report predicts. The underlying economics were neatly summarised by Navios Maritime Partners boss Angeliki Frangou during an August earnings call. “The longer ton-mile is like removing from the supply of vessels,” Frangou explained, pointing out that rerouting caused by the Red Sea and Hormuz crises meant ships were spending considerably longer at sea. Jan Rindbo, CEO of Norden, made a similar observation at last month’s Splash Singapore conference. “The world fleet is breaking down into smaller fleets,” Rindbo said, explaining how sanctions, regional conflicts and environmental regulations were fragmenting what was once a relatively unified global merchant fleet. The result is declining fleet efficiency, with more vessels required to transport the same quantities of cargo. Nikolas Tsakos, founder and CEO of Tsakos Energy Navigation, acknowledged the extraordinary opportunities created by the crisis during his company’s September earnings call. “This is uncharted territory, which we are taking advantage of carefully and steadily,” Tsakos said, while stressing his preference for peace even at the expense of today’s record returns. Jefferies believes the tanker rally has further to run, although not necessarily at today’s spectacular spot rates. The bank has lifted its 2027 VLCC earnings forecast from $60,000 to $65,000 a day and its LR2 projection from $30,000 to $34,000, arguing that persistent trading inefficiencies, ageing fleets and future oil inventory rebuilding will support earnings long after the current crisis subsides. It estimates that 51% of crude tankers are at least 15 years old, potentially helping absorb an orderbook equivalent to around 27% of the existing fleet. Not everyone shares that optimism. Norden’s Rindbo has warned that the tanker market could be approaching its peak, prompting the Danish group to reduce tanker exposure and redirect capital towards dry bulk. At Splash Singapore, Christoph Toepfer, CEO of Borealis Maritime, delivered an even starker warning. “The better the party, the worse is the hangover. We’re having a hell of a party right now,” he quipped. The question is how this extraordinary, record-breaking cycle ends. A remarkable chart from Clarksons Research, comparing today’s VLCC boom with previous peaks in capesizes, LNG carriers and container shipping, provides perspective. The current VLCC surge has reached around 17 times its long-term average, dwarfing the peaks recorded in earlier shipping cycles. Yet those previous booms eventually surrendered most of their extraordinary earnings premiums, often within just a few months. The VLCC line on the Clarksons chart ends at today’s extraordinary levels, leaving the subsequent trajectory unanswered. The industry’s history suggests that exceptional earnings eventually correct. What makes this cycle different is that nobody can confidently predict when the geopolitical distortions sustaining it will disappear, or how quickly an apparent shortage of tankers could turn into a surplus. articles.body: Europe Operations NATO boosts Black Sea surveillance amid attacks on shipping Adis Ajdin October 21, 2026 1 506 1 minute read NATO is deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, drones and radar systems to the Black Sea following a series of deadly attacks on merchant shipping off Romania and Bulgaria. The move follows a meeting of the alliance’s North Atlantic Council in Brussels on Tuesday, with members also sending intelligence personnel and explosives investigation teams to the region. NATO military spokesman colonel Martin O’Donnell said the additional assets would strengthen surveillance and reconnaissance, with the emphasis on improving intelligence sharing and identifying threats to shipping. Bulgaria has already confirmed that a US Navy P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft has begun reconnaissance flights over the Black Sea following its request for assistance from NATO. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev said allies had responded quickly to Sofia’s appeal, with further support expected. Four merchant ships have been attacked in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone over the past month, two of which sank. Allied specialists are also expected to help investigate the October 13 drone attack on the Malta-flagged general cargoship Chelsea 3 off Bulgaria. All 15 crewmembers were rescued, and investigators are examining recovered drone debris to establish the type of weapon used. The latest NATO response comes after a string of attacks on commercial vessels, including two chemical tankers off Romania last week. One of them, the Comoros-flagged Yara J , caught fire after a suspected drone strike inside Romanian territorial waters near the Sulina Canal. The crew managed to extinguish the blaze without outside assistance. The attacks have increasingly threatened shipping routes serving Ukraine’s Danube and Black Sea ports, adding to pressure on grain exports and pushing war-risk insurance costs higher. Russia’s defence ministry separately claimed on Tuesday that its forces had struck three cargo vessels at the Ukrainian port of Reni and another two heading towards Odesa, alleging that the ships were being used for military purposes. NATO has not formally attributed the recent attacks off Romania and Bulgaria to Russia, which has denied responsibility for those incidents. Despite the worsening security situation, Bulgarian authorities said commercial shipping to the Black Sea ports of Varna and Burgas was continuing, with no decline in vessel traffic reported. articles.title: Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years
articles.summary: Iraq’s national shipping line is returning to scheduled container services in the Gulf after more than half a century, as the country seeks to rebuild maritime connections disrupted by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. According to Alphaliner, Iraqi Maritime Line is deploying the 902 teu Basrah on an eight-day shuttle...
articles.body: Containers Middle East Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years Sam Chambers October 21, 2026 0 2,064 1 minute read ICTSI ICTSI Iraq’s national shipping line is returning to scheduled container services in the Gulf after more than half a century, as the country seeks to rebuild maritime connections disrupted by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. According to Alphaliner, Iraqi Maritime Line is deploying the 902 teu Basrah on an eight-day shuttle linking Jebel Ali in Dubai with Umm Qasr, Iraq’s principal container gateway. The first sailing was scheduled to depart Jebel Ali yesterday, arriving in Umm Qasr two days later. Iraq’s transport ministry has described the initiative as the national carrier’s first regular Gulf operation since the mid-1960s. The relaunch comes as Iraqi container supply chains have been radically reshaped since the Hormuz shipping crisis erupted at the end of February. Growing volumes have been diverted to Jordan’s Red Sea port of Aqaba before travelling overland into Iraq through the Trebil border crossing. According to the Jordan Shipping Association, Aqaba handled 37,182 Iraq-bound transit containers during the first seven months of 2026, compared with just 3,599 during the corresponding period last year, a 933% increase. Maersk has introduced landbridge services connecting Aqaba with Iraq, while CMA CGM has offered alternative routings through Aqaba for southern Iraq and Turkey’s Mersin for northern destinations. The French carrier has also established multimodal connections through Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah and ports in Oman and the UAE. Other carriers have maintained limited maritime connections through smaller feeder vessels. Hapag-Lloyd outlined a routing in July whereby containers are discharged at Khorfakkan, outside the Strait of Hormuz, before being trucked across the UAE to Sharjah or Jebel Ali and transferred onto third-party feeder vessels serving Iraq and other upper Gulf destinations. The new Iraqi service will provide a dedicated national shipping connection with the region’s largest container hub, although vessels operating between Jebel Ali and Umm Qasr must still navigate the increasingly dangerous Strait of Hormuz. The shuttle therefore complements rather than replaces the overland alternatives that have become vital to keeping Iraqi imports moving. According to Xclusiv Shipbrokers, the New York-listed owner has lined up two ships at the CSSC-controlled yard, priced at around $109m each, with delivery scheduled for 2029. Danaos has been a regular customer of Chinese shipyards in recent years, spreading orders across several builders as it renews and expands its containership fleet. The company already has seven 9,200 teu vessels under construction at other Chinese yards under contracts placed in 2024, with deliveries scheduled between 2027 and 2028. Its more recent investments include six 1,800 teu feeder vessels booked in November last year for delivery through 2029, followed by four 5,300 teu ships at CSSC Huangpu Wenchong, disclosed in February. Danaos’ latest corporate update, issued at the beginning of October, put its operating container fleet at 78 vessels totalling 502,265 teu, with another 28 newbuildings representing 177,776 teu of additional capacity. Beyond containers, Danaos has also been building a sizeable position in dry bulk. It owns 11 capesizes and has another four 211,000 dwt newcastlemaxes under construction at China’s Dajin Heavy Industry, representing an investment of about $297m. The group had been exploring a separate Oslo listing for its 15-ship bulker business, including a potential minority stake sale, as part of efforts to unlock value from the fleet. However, those plans have reportedly been put on hold after investor soundings failed to produce a satisfactory valuation amid weaker dry bulk freight rates and stock market conditions. Danaos has not formally confirmed the postponement or disclosed a revised timetable. articles.title: North Sea gas field cleared for take-off: UK greenlights Jackdaw after legal storms
articles.summary: The UK regulator has given Shell-backed Adura the go-ahead for a North Sea gas field following a courtroom showdown with environmental campaigners.
articles.body: Authorities & Government October 21, 2026 · 19 hours ago North Sea gas field cleared for take-off: UK greenlights Jackdaw after legal storms The UK regulator has given Shell-backed Adura the go-ahead for a North Sea gas field following a courtroom showdown with environmental campaigners. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 4 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Jackdaw platform Source: Aker Solutions One of the North Sea’s most controversial gas projects has clawed its way back from the courtroom after climate legal challenges threw its future into limbo. Adura, an incorporated joint venture between UK-headquartered Shell and Norway’s Equinor, has now secured clearance to push ahead with Jackdaw, a high-stakes field designed to heat millions of British homes, even as environmental battles look set to rage on. The North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA) has granted development and production consent for the Jackdaw field off the coast of northeast Scotland to Adura, following the SoS’ consideration of the company’s environmental statement and agreement to the grant of consent. Stuart Payn , NSTA’s Chief Executive, commented: “After robust scrutiny we have today granted consent for the Jackdaw field development which allows the owners to proceed with their project and produce gas from the field upon completion of development work. “This project will support the UK’s energy security by providing domestically produced gas, generate tax revenues, safeguard supply chain jobs, use existing infrastructure, and have an emissions intensity well below the UK average.” Jackdaw has the potential to deliver around 6% of projected UK North Sea gas production, which is considered to be enough fuel to heat the equivalent of 1.4 million homes at a time when older gas fields are reaching the end of their production. Payn added: "Now is the time to move forward at pace and we welcome the government's approval in allowing us permission to consider a small number of new out of round licences ahead of forthcoming legislation." The field, located approximately 250 kilometers east of Aberdeen, is expected to be among the lowest-emission developments on the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS), while supporting jobs and bolstering Britain’s energy security. Previously, the NSTA gave consent on June 1, 2022, to develop the Jackdaw project after the Offshore Petroleum Regulator for Environment & Decommissioning (OPRED) agreed to the grant of consent for the development following an assessment of the environmental impacts of the project. However, Greenpeace asked the Scottish Court to review the grant of consent and OPRED’s agreement to the grant of consent in relation to the planning application and the need to consider not only the emissions from the platform’s operations but also the emissions when the gas is used by customers. The UK Supreme Court issued a judgment in a case referred to as ‘Finch’ in 2024 , regarding a proposed oil well in Surrey that was approved by the local council in 2019, ruling that the approval should also have considered the emissions produced by the oil’s end use as well as those emissions caused by the oil well’s operations. Afterward, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled on January 30, 2025, that the previous government’s decision to approve the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil fields was unlawful. As a result, the court overturned the decision, accepting Uplift’s argument that the government failed to consider the emissions that would be caused by burning the oil and gas produced by these fields when it approved them. Related Articles Fossil Energy Multi-billion projects at stake: Another blow for UK’s largest untapped oil & gas duo but Shell, Equinor, and Ithaca remain upbeat 14 min read Adura has continued to comply with all laws and regulations relating to the Jackdaw project situated in blocks 30/02a, 30/03a, and 30/02d of the United Kingdom Continental Shelf that lies in a water depth of approximately 78 meters. The field is located in the Central North Sea (CNS), 30 kilometers southeast of the Shearwater platform and adjacent to the UK/Norway median line. Jackdaw is a gas/condensate development comprising a not permanently attended wellhead platform with four wells, tied back to the Shearwater hub via a 31-kilometer pipeline. The steel jacket and topside were installed in August 2023 and October 2025, respectively. The pipeline was laid in July 2024 and the drilling activities were completed in early 2026. While the latest approval marks a major turning point, the environmental battles are not entirely over since environmental groups like Greenpeace remain strongly opposed to the development of the North Sea oil and gas projects, which have become a primary battleground for climate litigation. As a result, activists continue to scrutinize these approvals. By resubmitting the required environmental statements and clearing this regulatory hurdle, the Jackdaw project has overcome the specific legal blockades that previously stalled it, allowing developers to finally move forward even if political and activist friction persists. Responding to the government giving the Jackdaw gas field the go-ahead, Sam Richards , CEO of Britain Remade, said: “Britain is going to need gas for decades to come, as even the Climate Change Committee recognises. The choice is not between gas and no gas, but between gas produced in British waters and gas shipped in from abroad at higher cost and with higher emissions. “But while we should use what we have, the North Sea is a declining basin, and we need to transition to homegrown clean power. Britain’s always-on electricity should come from new clean nuclear, both gigawatt-scale reactors and small modular reactors that can be sited in far more places than their bigger cousins. “Right now Britain is the most expensive place in the world to build new nuclear. Ministers should urgently implement the Fingleton Review in full in order to drive down cost. The government should also commit to a new small modular reactor at Dungeness without delay.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! The Danilo Fumarola-led company has booked the trio for delivery between late 2028 and early 2029, expanding beyond its traditional panamax and kamsarmax fleet. The newbuilding deal adds another international owner to Nantong Xiangyu’s growing customer base.
